articles.title: Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students
articles.summary:

The post Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under.

In March 2020, COVID lockdowns shuttered schools around the world, including at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, where Prince Bashangezi was completing his A-Level studies. The camp sits near the Mozambique border, home to more than 17,000 people displaced by conflict across central and eastern Africa. Formal schooling stopped. Prince and a group of fellow A-Level students at USAP Community School, a school serving refugee youth in the camp, decided not to wait for it to resume.

They founded TWEENS: Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. The model was built around what they had: each other.

Teaching from inside the camp

TWEENS began as a service learning project, with refugee students tutoring younger students in the same camp. The premise was direct. These were students who understood exactly what it meant to study without resources, without stability, often without continuous access to teachers, and in many cases without families to support them. They knew the particular difficulty of trying to build a future from inside a displaced population. So they taught each other.

The program was supported by Education Matters Africa, a Zimbabwe-based nonprofit, and launched at a moment when any alternative to organized education was better than none. What began during a global lockdown became something that outlasted it.

Prince was also a Waterford Kamhlaba UWC of Southern Africa alumnus, a school known for selecting students across conflict zones and economic hardship who show unusual potential and commitment. That network eventually connected him to the Global Student Haven Initiative at Pomona College in California, where he now studies computer science and economics.

Marianne Langridge, who nominated Prince for this series, wrote that he “has turned his personal tragedy of losing his family during war into loving service for others.” That framing, loss converted into something that benefits others, runs through how Prince has talked about his work and what TWEENS is for. Langridge described his commitment as rooted in wanting students in refugee camps to “gain access to education so they can have hope for a better future.”

Why peer tutoring works here

There is something specific about a peer model in a refugee context that a standard school or aid program can’t replicate. The tutors in TWEENS are not professionals, not volunteers flying in from outside, not people working from a comfortable distance. They are students who live where the students they’re teaching live. They went through the same disruptions. Their credibility comes from proximity, not credentials.

This is similar in structure to the peer-learning model that makes other youth-run programs effective, but in a refugee camp the stakes of educational continuity are different. A child who falls significantly behind in a displacement context faces a compounding disadvantage. Keeping any educational thread alive, even an informal one built by A-Level students during a lockdown, matters more than it might in a setting with backup resources. TWEENS was built on that understanding.

From Tongogara to Pomona

Prince arrived at Pomona College through the Global Student Haven Initiative, which supports students from refugee and displaced communities. He is studying computer science and economics, a combination that maps directly to the problems TWEENS is trying to solve: how technology and resource allocation interact to either expand or cut off access to education.

Pomona profiled him in 2024 as part of a piece on Global Haven students finding opportunity in higher education. A fundraising campaign on GlobalGiving continues to support TWEENS’ operations, keeping the peer tutoring program funded as he completes his degree.

What Prince Bashangezi and his fellow students built during a lockdown in a refugee camp, with nothing but time and knowledge and the willingness to share both, is still running more than five years later. TWEENS now offers an A-level program, a girls’ book club, and ongoing homework support alongside its original peer tutoring. To support TWEENS, visit their GlobalGiving fundraising page.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

Supported by a local nonprofit, Education Matters Africa, TWEENS began during the lockdown and continued afterward, expanding its activities.

**Impact** – The program’s strength comes from tutors who live in the same challenging conditions as their students. articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2020, las escuelas cerraron en todo el mundo por el COVID-19, incluyendo el campamento de refugiados Tongogara en Zimbabue. articles.title: Justice is the infrastructure the world keeps forgetting
articles.summary: Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted.
articles.content:
This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms. We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare. Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.

We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities. We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.

This institutional obsession reflects a deeper failure in how we understand development. Justice is not simply a legal service or a moral aspiration. It is essential for economic and social infrastructure. Our collective failure to treat it as such is undermining development, deepening inequality and threatening global stability. With the level of discontent across the world, distrust in institutions, poverty and inequality, and growing footprints of violent conflict, we need to refocus on what is necessary to heal our bleeding world.

The missing infrastructure of development

When governments and international financial institutions discuss infrastructure, the conversation invariably turns to roads, bridges, electricity and digital connectivity. These investments matter. But what happens when a highway project becomes trapped in unresolved land disputes; when a small business cannot recover payments from a supplier? When a woman cannot claim her inheritance, or communities cannot secure remedies for environmental destruction?

Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted. Justice is the soft infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function.

For businesses, it provides the certainty necessary for investment, contract enforcement and growth. For individuals, it protects rights, livelihoods and opportunities. For communities, it creates peaceful pathways for addressing grievances before they escalate into confrontation.

Without functioning justice systems, economic development becomes fragile and social stability increasingly precarious. The World Justice Project estimates that the economic costs of legal problems, including lost income, health impacts and expenses of seeking resolution, average 1.7 percent of GDP across the countries studied.

The scale of the problem is staggering. The Justice for All report estimates that 5.2 billion people lack meaningful access to justice. HiiL's research demonstrates that everyday legal problems are widespread, while effective, satisfactory resolutions remain elusive. This is a crisis of development.

When injustice becomes insecurity

Across the world, unresolved grievances are quietly eroding the foundations of social cohesion.

In parts of Africa, disputes over land ownership, natural resources and community rights have contributed to recurring tensions. In fragile and conflict-affected societies, the absence of credible mechanisms for resolving grievances can deepen mistrust and reinforce cycles of violence.

But justice failures are hardly confined to developing countries. From housing disputes and discriminatory employment practices to unequal access to legal representation, even wealthy democracies struggle to ensure that justice works for everyone.

The consequences extend beyond those directly affected. When people repeatedly encounter institutions that cannot protect their rights or resolve their problems, confidence in public authority deteriorates. When people encounter injustice, they can easily become the enemy of the state. And where legitimate institutions fail, alternative systems of enforcement emerge. Sometimes these are constructive community mechanisms. At other times, they involve coercion, exploitation or violence. We cannot sustainably address insecurity while ignoring the injustices that help fuel it.

This should fundamentally change how governments approach peacebuilding and security. Military and policing investments may respond to immediate threats, but accessible justice can help address grievances before they become security crises.

Justice should therefore be understood as preventive infrastructure, not merely a mechanism for responding to wrongdoing after it occurs.

What the evidence tells us

Fortunately, evidence from across HiiL’s global operations demonstrates how people-centred approaches are transforming the design and delivery of justice services. Rather than relying solely on formal courtrooms or conventional approaches to conflict resolution, community-led initiatives and alternative justice pathways are meeting people where their disputes actually occur.

In Kenya, research informed the Judiciary’s Social Transformation through Access to Justice (STAJ) Blueprint. The Alternative Justice Systems (AJS) centres in Kenya are resolving family, land and other disputes locally, thereby preserving community cohesion. In Ethiopia, government-led community justice centers bridge formal laws and customary traditions to deliver rapid, reconciliation-focused resolution. In Nigeria, pilot community justice centers and domestic violence one-stop shops in Imo and Ogun States provide scalable, data-driven dispute resolution. In Tunisia, digital platforms co-developed for employment disputes directly connect workers, employers, and inspectors to resolve conflicts before they escalate.

Instead of assuming what institutions need, the question is: What justice problems do people actually experience, and what would help resolve them fairly?

Through Justice Needs and Satisfaction (JNS) surveys, we gather data on everyday legal experiences rather than institutional outputs. The data consistently reveal a significant disconnect between supply and demand. In Tunisia, we found that nearly one in three adults experiences a legal problem annually, yet only a fraction reach formal courts. Similarly, research in Nigeria highlights widespread justice needs alongside heavy reliance on community and informal mechanisms. These insights expose the core limitation of traditional justice reform: expanding court capacity alone cannot solve the problem. People facing family, land, employment, or commercial disputes rarely seek lengthy litigation. They need solutions that are fair, accessible, affordable, and timely.

Similar approaches are yielding results. In Bangladesh, a government-led initiative has strengthened village courts, enabling rural communities to resolve minor disputes locally, more quickly and affordably. These courts resolved over 82 percent of reported cases in an average of 25 days, at an average cost of just USD 2.70 to users. In Canada, the Indigenous Justice Program supports community-based initiatives that involve Indigenous communities in designing and delivering culturally appropriate justice services, reflecting their needs and traditions. In Colombia, Houses of Justice bring together formal and informal justice services, providing communities with access to legal information, mediation and dispute resolution through integrated service centres. These examples illustrate how justice services can be brought closer to people and organised around different pathways to better respond to their needs.

This does not make courts obsolete; rather, it underscores that formal courts are only one component of a healthy justice ecosystem. To truly serve society, functional justice infrastructure must integrate formal institutions with trusted community mechanisms, mediation, legal support, and innovative services.

From justice reform to justice investment

If justice is infrastructure, we must fundamentally rethink how we finance, govern and deliver it.

First, governments must stop treating justice as the Ministry of Justice's exclusive responsibility. Economic planners, finance ministries, development institutions, businesses and peacebuilding organisations all have a stake in effective dispute resolution.

Second, justice investments must be guided by evidence about people's needs and outcomes. HiiL's Delivering Justice, Rigorously framework emphasises data, evidence-based practices, scalable services, enabling environments, and accountability.

Third, we must move beyond endless small-scale pilots towards financing solutions that demonstrate results and can reach entire populations. The Justice Financing Framework developed under the Justice Action Coalition offers important proposals for making people-centred justice services financially sustainable.

Finally, justice must become integral to development financing. International financial institutions and development partners should recognize that investments in agriculture, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, gender equality and peacebuilding depend partly on people’s ability to resolve disputes fairly and the credibility of the entire justice system. This is not an argument for diverting resources from development priorities. It is an argument for making those investments more effective and sustainable.

The foundation we cannot afford to ignore

The world faces intersecting crises of inequality, economic uncertainty, democratic distrust and violent conflict. Governments are searching for ways to build more resilient societies, yet one of the most important foundations of resilience remains chronically neglected.

Justice cannot continue to be treated as an institutional afterthought.

A society is not resilient simply because it has strong borders, modern highways or growing financial markets. It is resilient when people trust that grievances can be addressed fairly, rights can be protected, and conflicts can be resolved without violence.

The question is no longer whether we can afford to invest in people-centred justice. It is whether we can afford the economic, social and political consequences of failing to do so. This spotlight provides the argument for the justice case, evidence of what is working and a roadmap of what we must do to make justice work for our societies.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the critical role of justice as essential infrastructure for societal stability, economic development, and peacebuilding. It presents evidence-based, people-centered justice reforms and community-led initiatives across multiple countries that improve access to justice for billions of people. The story addresses a broad, significant issue affecting global populations and offers concrete examples and frameworks for scalable solutions, making it an inspiring and hopeful call for systemic change.
articles.personality_title: Justice as essential infrastructure: How fair dispute resolution supports societies worldwide
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many countries focus on building physical infrastructure like roads and bridges but often overlook justice systems that help resolve disputes and protect rights. Without accessible and trusted justice, other developments struggle to succeed.

**What happened** – Organizations like The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) and Global Voices are highlighting how justice acts as critical infrastructure. They share examples from countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Tunisia, Bangladesh, Canada, and Colombia, where community-based and people-centered justice programs are making it easier for millions to solve legal problems fairly and quickly.

**Impact** – These new approaches show that justice is more than courts and laws—it is about creating trusted ways for people to settle disputes and protect their rights. When justice works well, it supports business growth, social peace, and equality. For example, village courts in Bangladesh resolve most cases in under a month at low cost, and Indigenous programs in Canada respect cultural traditions while delivering justice.

**What's next step** – Experts say governments and international groups must treat justice like other infrastructure by investing more, using data to guide reforms, and expanding successful local solutions. This means involving not just legal bodies but also finance ministries and development organizations to ensure justice systems grow stronger and reach more people.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Treating justice as essential infrastructure and investing in community-focused solutions helps build fairer, safer, and more stable societies worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: La justice, une infrastructure essentielle pour soutenir les sociétés dans le monde entier
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux pays se concentrent sur la construction d’infrastructures physiques comme les routes et les ponts, mais négligent souvent les systèmes de justice qui aident à résoudre les conflits et protéger les droits. Sans une justice accessible et digne de confiance, les autres développements peinent à réussir.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des organisations comme l’Institut de La Haye pour l’Innovation du Droit (HiiL) et Global Voices soulignent que la justice est une infrastructure cruciale. Elles présentent des exemples de pays tels que le Kenya, l’Éthiopie, le Nigeria, la Tunisie, le Bangladesh, le Canada et la Colombie, où des programmes de justice communautaire et centrés sur les personnes facilitent la résolution équitable et rapide des problèmes juridiques pour des millions de personnes.

**Impact** – Ces nouvelles approches montrent que la justice ne se limite pas aux tribunaux et aux lois : il s’agit de créer des moyens fiables pour que les gens règlent leurs différends et protègent leurs droits. Quand la justice fonctionne bien, elle soutient la croissance économique, la paix sociale et l’égalité. Par exemple, les tribunaux de village au Bangladesh règlent la plupart des affaires en moins d’un mois à faible coût, et les programmes pour les peuples autochtones au Canada respectent les traditions culturelles tout en assurant la justice.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les experts affirment que les gouvernements et les organisations internationales doivent considérer la justice comme une infrastructure à part entière en investissant davantage, en utilisant les données pour guider les réformes, et en étendant les solutions locales réussies. Cela implique d’impliquer non seulement les organismes juridiques, mais aussi les ministères des finances et les organisations de développement pour renforcer les systèmes de justice et les rendre accessibles à tous.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Traiter la justice comme une infrastructure essentielle et investir dans des solutions centrées sur les communautés aide à construire des sociétés plus justes, sûres et stables dans le monde entier.
articles.personality_title_es: La justicia como infraestructura esencial: cómo la resolución justa de conflictos sostiene a las sociedades en todo el mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos países se enfocan en construir infraestructura física como carreteras y puentes, pero a menudo pasan por alto los sistemas de justicia que ayudan a resolver disputas y proteger derechos. Sin una justicia accesible y confiable, otros desarrollos tienen dificultades para avanzar.

**Qué pasó** – Organizaciones como el Instituto de La Haya para la Innovación Legal (HiiL) y Global Voices destacan cómo la justicia funciona como infraestructura crítica. Presentan ejemplos de países como Kenia, Etiopía, Nigeria, Túnez, Bangladesh, Canadá y Colombia, donde programas comunitarios y centrados en las personas facilitan que millones resuelvan problemas legales de manera justa y rápida.

**Impacto** – Estos nuevos enfoques muestran que la justicia es más que tribunales y leyes: es crear formas confiables para que las personas solucionen sus conflictos y protejan sus derechos. Cuando la justicia funciona bien, apoya el crecimiento económico, la paz social y la igualdad. Por ejemplo, los tribunales de aldeas en Bangladesh resuelven la mayoría de los casos en menos de un mes y a bajo costo, y los programas indígenas en Canadá respetan tradiciones culturales mientras brindan justicia.

**Próximo paso** – Los expertos dicen que los gobiernos y las organizaciones internacionales deben tratar la justicia como infraestructura, invirtiendo más, usando datos para guiar reformas y ampliando soluciones locales exitosas. Esto requiere involucrar no solo a los organismos legales, sino también a ministerios de finanzas y organizaciones de desarrollo para fortalecer los sistemas de justicia y hacerlos accesibles para más personas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Tratar la justicia como infraestructura esencial e invertir en soluciones centradas en la comunidad ayuda a construir sociedades más justas, seguras y estables en todo el mundo.

articles.title: In Ukraine, youth are finding their voices in the digital democracy
articles.summary: We saw a gap: young people were consuming information and even participating online, but without media literacy, digital security awareness, or confidence that their voice could shape anything.
articles.content:
This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

The war in Ukraine has created a myriad of challenges for youth and their participation in public life and democratic processes, bringing displacement and misinformation as well as decreased opportunities for political engagement, economic activity, and access to information. At the same time, there are still avenues youth can pursue to contribute to political decisions and shape the fate of their communities.

Despite the war, people can still submit petitions, participate in public consultations, or advocate for their needs online, but there is a lack of awareness about such opportunities. Furthermore, vulnerable groups — including displaced persons, minorities, and rural communities — know they have a voice, but struggle to find it.

In 2026, the local non-governmental organization beYOUnd implemented a project to help youth from vulnerable groups acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to find their voices in this new era of digital democracy. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Yevheniia Holovenko, the chairwoman of beYOUnd, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Yevheniia Holovenko (YH): beYOUnd is a youth-led NGO based in Ukraine, registered in October 2025, though we’ve worked as a team long before that. Our mission is to increase the involvement of vulnerable youth, especially internally displaced people and young people facing difficult social and economic circumstances, in integration, self-realization, and civic life. Our name reflects our philosophy: it starts with you; it goes beyond! Our team is largely made up of young people who’ve lived through the same challenges as the youth we work with, which shapes how we approach everything we do. We joined the Digital Sparks initiative because digital democracy and civic space are exactly where Ukrainian youth need support right now. Safe, informed participation online is inseparable from resilience during war, and it matched our mission perfectly.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

YH: The war has pushed many young Ukrainians, especially internally displaced persons (IDPs), into digital spaces to stay connected, informed, and civically active, often without the tools to do so safely. We saw a gap: young people were consuming information and even participating online, but without media literacy, digital security awareness, or confidence that their voice could shape anything. We wanted to close this gap by developing practical digital safety and civic participation skills in displaced and marginalized youth. We wanted to give them an opportunity to share ideas on how to increase awareness of digital democracy with the involvement of young people in Ukraine.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

YH: Within the project “Voices of Democracy in the Digital Era,” we ran an awareness campaign covering digital security, e-participation, and disinformation, which reached over 8,500 views. On the education side, we delivered three webinars and three workshops on digital democracy, media literacy, civic action planning, and cybersecurity, engaging over a hundred participants. We also organized an offline networking event in the capital, Kyiv, bringing 27 participants together in person to connect around these same topics, and build on the online learning with real, face-to-face relationships and exchange. Together, these activities, which combined online reach with in-person community building, gave young people both the knowledge and the network to act on this newly acquired knowledge.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

YH: “Voices of Democracy” reshaped how our beneficiaries see their own place in their community. As one participant shared, “I discovered new digital tools I can use to engage with my community and take part in important decisions.” Others said the most valuable part was learning how to protect their personal data and use digital services safely in everyday life. Several highlighted finally understanding the difference between advocacy and broader civic action, and how to build a real plan for their own initiative — skills that came alive through teamwork. As another participant put it, “I learned to define a problem, trace its causes, and plan real steps to solve it — and I understood better what advocacy is and how it can drive positive change in a community.” For many, this changed how they see their own ability to influence change locally.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

YH: Leading this project deepened our understanding of how closely digital safety and democratic participation are linked. You can’t meaningfully engage young people in civic life online without first equipping them to navigate that space securely. Working alongside experts in digital security and civic engagement broadened our grasp of practical tools we now use, and how we think about beYOUnd’s programming. It also pushed us to see capacity-building more structurally: not just what we teach beneficiaries, but how we build our own organizational resilience for the long term, not just on a project-by-project basis.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

YH: The biggest lesson was that combining practical, hands-on content with real interaction (webinars, workshops, and offline networking) worked far better than any one format alone. Participants didn’t just absorb information; they built relationships and confidence to act on it, especially through the in-person exchange in Kyiv. We also learned how much value there is in simple, clear, practical content. Participants consistently said what stuck with them most was information they could immediately use, not abstract theory. Finally, working through capacity-building for our own team alongside the project reminded us that organizational resilience matters just as much as the skills we pass on to beneficiaries.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

articles.title: Metascience should be a source of evidence, not a means of control
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03620-zThe field has captured the interest of politicians. There are positives — but governments must not misuse the data.
articles.content:
The field has captured the interest of politicians. There are positives — but governments must not misuse the data.

Efforts to apply metascience to research funding must put evidence and scientists front and centre.Credit: Alamy

The European Research Council made headlines last month when the news broke that those applying for one of its core grants had only a 5% chance of success. Partly as a result of applicants using artificial intelligence, the ratio of submissions to grants at the European Union’s premier science funder is now so skewed as to be little more than a lottery. Some funders are already using lotteries to select grant recipients, viewing these as a fairer way to allocate funding.

More self-reflection in research can lead to better science

This is not a coincidence. The idea of distributing certain types of grant randomly has been tested experimentally over a number of years. It’s one example of how the field of metascience — the study of the practice of science itself — is having a real-world impact.

Metascience is not new. The world’s oldest journal devoted to the study of science, Nauka Polska, based in Poland, was founded in 1918 and is still publishing. Nature frequently reports on metascience, invites researchers to share their opinions and publishes primary science in the field. A set of studies released in April, for example, investigated the reproducibility, replicability and robustness of research in the social and behavioural sciences1–4. Developments in research funding, research organization, communication and evaluation are all aspects of metascience.

Metascience is also used by governments to support policy and funding decisions. In the past few years, a number of governments have established and funded metascience research units, as detailed in Seize the Meta Moment, a review by an international group of researchers and policymakers that was published last week by the Research on Research Institute in London (see go.nature.com/4z7pdt1). The author list includes members of some of these government-funded metascience units.

Huge meta-research project puts claims in social-science papers to the test

In one sense, this is positive, an example of policymakers seeking solutions informed by research. But the review’s authors point out that political attention also introduces risks — namely that the discipline could be misused to serve government agendas or to justify decisions that are not supported by a consensus of the evidence. They acknowledge that metascience will, to some extent, always be political, but that this should be acknowledged. And they urge politicians to use metascience as a learning tool and a source of evidence, but not as a means of controlling researchers.

In the United States, the Office of Science and Technology Policy has tasked all federal science agencies with establishing metascience capabilities. This was outlined in a July report, Science: A New Golden Age, which criticized excessive bureaucracy and slowness in US science, and embraced the idea of accelerating grant-awarding processes (see go.nature.com/3uj6pf5). One concern is that the US administration could use metascience to push through major changes, such as funding cuts, support for higher-risk research or the adoption of AI, without engaging the broader scientific community.

I built the UK government’s metascience unit — here’s what countries need to know

The United States is not the only country where researchers are worried about potential metascience misuse; concerns have also been raised in the United Kingdom, the first country to establish a government metascience unit. Last year, the nation’s main public funder of social science, the Economic and Social Research Council, announced a commitment to promoting economic growth. This is part of a broader economic push by the nation’s main public funder, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), in response to a government priority.

The extent to which publicly funded science contributes to growth and the mechanisms underlying it are well-studied questions in the social sciences, and there are a range of views both supporting and critiquing the UK government’s objectives. It’s important that funders such as UKRI do not align themselves with just one view, and that the metascience unit does not reduce measurement of grant recipients’ performance to a metric that is itself still a matter of debate in the research community.

Why science has a credibility problem — and how to address it

Most of the world’s science funding agencies were established when research careers were accessible to relatively few people. There is now a much larger and more mobile pool of researchers due, in part, to the expansion of universities and the globalization of science. Funding agencies need to change how they work to adapt as the world changes. That includes addressing the problem of falling success rates resulting from the greater demand for grants.

By far the best way for policymakers to use metascience to inform funding decisions is for them to work with researchers to create and implement tools designed to measure quality and competitiveness, and — as in science itself — to learn from experimentation and experience.

articles.personality_title: Metascience helps improve how science funding is decided, but must be used carefully
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Metascience is the study of how science is done, including how research is funded and evaluated. It has gained attention from governments wanting to make science funding fairer and more effective.

**What happened** – Recently, the European Research Council revealed that only 5% of science grant applications are successful, partly because many use artificial intelligence to apply. Some funders have started using lotteries to decide who gets grants, as a fairer way to choose. Governments in the US, UK, and Europe are creating special teams to study metascience and guide science policies.

**Impact** – Using metascience helps make funding decisions more evidence-based and can improve the quality and fairness of research support. For example, testing lotteries shows new ways to allocate grants more fairly. However, there is a risk that governments might misuse this information to control scientists or push certain agendas without enough input from researchers.

**What's next step** – Experts say governments should work closely with scientists to develop fair tools for measuring research quality. They advise careful use of metascience to guide policies, ensuring it supports open, balanced decisions rather than controlling researchers.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Metascience offers new ways to improve how science funding works, but it must be used carefully to support fair and honest research.
articles.personality_title_fr: La métascience améliore le financement de la recherche, mais doit être utilisée avec prudence
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La métascience étudie la manière dont la science est pratiquée, notamment le financement et l’évaluation de la recherche. Elle attire l’attention des gouvernements qui veulent rendre le financement scientifique plus juste et efficace.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Récemment, le Conseil européen de la recherche a révélé que seulement 5 % des demandes de subvention sont acceptées, en partie à cause de l’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle. Certains financeurs utilisent désormais des tirages au sort pour attribuer les subventions, estimant que c’est plus équitable. Des équipes spécialisées en métascience ont été créées aux États-Unis, au Royaume-Uni et en Europe pour orienter les politiques scientifiques.

**Impact** – La métascience permet de prendre des décisions basées sur des preuves, améliorant la qualité et l’équité du financement. Par exemple, tester des tirages au sort montre de nouvelles façons plus justes d’attribuer les subventions. Cependant, il existe un risque que les gouvernements utilisent ces données pour contrôler les chercheurs ou imposer des choix sans consulter suffisamment la communauté scientifique.

**Prochaine étape** – Les experts conseillent aux gouvernements de collaborer étroitement avec les scientifiques pour créer des outils justes d’évaluation de la recherche. Ils recommandent d’utiliser la métascience avec prudence pour appuyer des décisions ouvertes et équilibrées, sans contrôler les chercheurs.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La métascience ouvre de nouvelles voies pour améliorer le financement de la science, à condition d’être utilisée avec soin pour soutenir une recherche juste et honnête.
articles.personality_title_es: La metaciencia mejora la financiación de la ciencia, pero debe usarse con cuidado
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La metaciencia estudia cómo se hace la ciencia, incluyendo cómo se financia y evalúa la investigación. Los gobiernos están interesados en ella para hacer que la financiación científica sea más justa y efectiva.

**Qué pasó** – Recientemente, el Consejo Europeo de Investigación informó que solo el 5 % de las solicitudes de subvenciones tienen éxito, en parte por el uso de inteligencia artificial. Algunos financiadores han empezado a usar loterías para decidir quién recibe subvenciones, ya que consideran que es un método más justo. Estados Unidos, Reino Unido y Europa están creando equipos especiales para estudiar la metaciencia y guiar las políticas científicas.

**Impacto** – La metaciencia ayuda a tomar decisiones basadas en evidencias, mejorando la calidad y equidad del apoyo a la investigación. Por ejemplo, probar loterías muestra nuevas formas más justas de asignar fondos. Sin embargo, existe el riesgo de que los gobiernos usen esta información para controlar a los científicos o impulsar ciertas agendas sin suficiente participación de los investigadores.

**Próximo paso** – Los expertos recomiendan que los gobiernos trabajen en colaboración con los científicos para crear herramientas justas para medir la calidad de la investigación. Aconsejan usar la metaciencia con cuidado para apoyar decisiones abiertas y equilibradas, sin controlar a los investigadores.

**Resumen en una frase** – La metaciencia ofrece nuevas maneras de mejorar la financiación de la ciencia, pero debe usarse con cuidado para apoyar una investigación justa y honesta.
